components.note: 尤 (particularly/outstanding) — relates to 就's sense of approaching or arriving at a particular point
京 (jīng, capital) gives a sound close to 就's pronunciation jiù
女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.hanzi: 火车就要开了,快点!
example.pinyin: Huǒchē jiùyào kāi le, kuài diǎn!
example.english: The train is about to leave, hurry up!
example.fact: 就要 almost always partners with a following 了 to mark an event as imminent ("就要...了") — dropping the 了 breaks the "about to happen" reading entirely, one of several Chinese time markers (also 快要...了, 要...了) built the same way.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拒 describes pushing something away with the hand, refusing.
巨 (jù) is an exact match for the sound of 拒.
纟 (thread) — 绝 originally meant to sever a thread completely, extended to mean 'to cut off, absolute'
色 (sè) gives a loose sound connection to 绝's reading jué

example.hanzi: 她拒绝了他的邀请。
example.pinyin: Tā jùjuéle tā de yāoqǐng.
example.english: She turned down his invitation.
example.fact: Its two halves are near-synonyms doubled for emphasis: 拒 alone (a hand 扌 pushing away) already means "to resist, push back," and 绝 (a thread 纟 severed clean through) already means "to cut off completely" — 拒绝 layers "push away" onto "cut off" for a forceful, unambiguous refusal.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 春节的时候,家人会聚在一起吃饭。
example.pinyin: Chūnjié de shíhou, jiārén huì jù zài yìqǐ chīfàn.
example.english: During Chinese New Year, family members gather together to eat.
example.fact: 家人 names the people who make up one's family (parents, siblings, etc.), while 家庭 names the family as an institution or household unit — a distinction close to English "family members" vs. "the family," though Chinese keeps the two nouns more strictly apart than English does.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 演 originally described water flowing and spreading out, later extended to 'developing, unfolding'
寅 (yín) gives a sound distantly related to 演's reading yǎn, having drifted apart over time
贝 (shell/money — cowrie shells were historically used as currency) — 员 originally related to counting or officials responsible for accounts, later broadening to mean 'member' or 'personnel.'

example.hanzi: 她是一位很有名的演员。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yí wèi hěn yǒumíng de yǎnyuán.
example.english: She is a very famous actor.
example.fact: 员 is a common suffix marking a person's occupation or role within a group — the same 员 turns up in 服务员 ("waiter, attendant") and 人员 (also in this batch, "personnel"), roughly parallel to the English suffix "-er" or "-ist" for professions.

components.note: 直 (straight, upright) — 真 relates to something level and true.
几 (a small table) — an object placed level and true on a table gave 真 its meaning 'real' or 'true.'

example.hanzi: 这是一个真实的故事。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè zhēnshí de gùshi.
example.english: This is a true story.
example.fact: 真实 fuses two overlapping near-synonyms for "genuine" (真 "true, real" plus 实 "solid, actual") into one adjective — the same two-near-synonym word-building strategy shows up elsewhere in this batch in 停止 and 允许, where a word doubles up two words of very close meaning rather than picking just one.

components.note: Depicts a person standing with legs crossed — the crossing shape gave 交 its meaning 'to intersect, exchange, hand over.'

example.hanzi: 这笔交易很成功。
example.pinyin: Zhè bǐ jiāoyì hěn chénggōng.
example.english: This transaction was very successful.
example.fact: 交易 takes 笔 as its measure word (一笔交易, "a transaction"), as its own dictionary entry notes, rather than the default 个 — 笔, literally "a stroke of the pen," is reserved for money-related or written transactions (also 一笔钱, "a sum of money"), a case where a measure word carries its own semantic flavor.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 停 relates to a person coming to a halt
亭 (tíng) gives the sound — an exact match with 停's reading tíng
止 depicts a footprint, with toes at the top and the leg below — a simple picture of a foot, later extended to mean 'to stop.'

example.hanzi: 雨已经停止了。
example.pinyin: Yǔ yǐjīng tíngzhǐ le.
example.english: The rain has already stopped.
example.fact: 止 on its own is a simple pictograph of a footprint, per its own component note, while 停 depicts a person (亻) coming to a halt — 停止 layers two independent old images of "stopping," one from a foot and one from a person, into a single emphatic verb.

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.hanzi: 人生就像一场旅行。
example.pinyin: Rénshēng jiù xiàng yì chǎng lǚxíng.
example.english: Life is like a journey.
example.fact: 人生 frames "life" as a lived, reflective arc — one's whole span of experience — while the everyday word 生活 means "life" in the practical sense of day-to-day living; a sentence about "the meaning of life" reaches for 人生, but "how's life going" reaches for 生活.

components.note: 匕 here relates to a person crouching or sitting — 此 originally pictured 'this place' where someone is.
止 (zhǐ) gives a hint of the sound — 此 is pronounced cǐ, sharing a similar final though the initial has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 他生病了,因此没能来上课。
example.pinyin: Tā shēngbìng le, yīncǐ méi néng lái shàngkè.
example.english: He got sick, so he wasn't able to come to class.
example.fact: 因此 is a more formal, written-register substitute for 所以 ("so, therefore") — both link a cause to its result, but 因此 shows up far more often in essays, reports, and speeches than in relaxed conversation, where 所以 still dominates.

meanings: variant of 惡心|恶心[e3 xin1]

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恶 relates to an evil or malicious state of heart/mind
亚 (yà) gives a sound distantly related to 恶's reading è, having drifted apart over time
心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.hanzi: 那个味道让我觉得很恶心。
example.pinyin: Nàge wèidào ràng wǒ juéde hěn ěxīn.
example.english: That smell makes me feel really nauseous.
example.fact: 恶 carries three unrelated-sounding readings depending on the word: è for "evil" (恶魔, "demon"), wù for "to hate, detest" (可恶, "hateful"), and ě only in this one word, 恶心, for "nauseous, disgusting" — a case where a character's pronunciation has to be learned word by word rather than predicted from a single rule.

components.note: 爫 (a hand, from above) — 受 pictures something being passed.
又 (a hand, from below) — one hand giving and another receiving gave 受 its meaning 'to receive' or 'to endure.'

example.hanzi: 他在比赛中受伤了。
example.pinyin: Tā zài bǐsài zhōng shòushāng le.
example.english: He got injured during the competition.
example.fact: 受 (also seen standalone in 感受, also in this batch) works as a Chinese verb prefix meaning "to receive, undergo" — 受伤 is literally "to receive an injury," always framing its subject as the one something happens to, close in spirit to English's passive "to be injured" even without an explicit passive marker like 被.

components.note: 女 (woman) — reflects the gender-specific reference of the term.
表 (biǎo) gives the sound — 婊 is also pronounced biǎo, an exact match.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 那部电视剧里,有人骂女主角是“婊子”。
example.pinyin: Nà bù diànshìjù lǐ, yǒurén mà nǚzhǔjué shì “biǎozi”.
example.english: In that TV drama, someone calls the female lead a "whore."
example.fact: 婊子 is a strongly vulgar, offensive insult in Mandarin, roughly on par with its English gloss — it turns up often in fiction, drama dialogue, and online arguments to paint a character as crude, but it is not a word to reach for casually in real conversation; the character 婊 itself rarely appears outside this word and its close slang derivatives.

components.note: 尸 (body) — ties to 属's sense of belonging to a category or class of related things
禹 (yǔ) gives a loose sound connection to 属's reading shǔ

example.hanzi: 这本书属于图书馆。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū shǔyú túshūguǎn.
example.english: This book belongs to the library.
example.fact: 属于 always takes the owner or category directly as its object (X属于Y, "X belongs to Y") — unlike English "belong," which needs the extra word "to," Chinese 属于 is never split into a separate verb plus preposition; 于 already fuses that "to" meaning onto 属.

components.note: 無-shaped top pictures a dancer holding decorated sleeves or fans.
舛 below pictures a pair of feet, together giving 舞 its meaning 'to dance.'
足 (foot) — 蹈 describes stepping or treading, an action of the foot.
舀 (yǎo) gives a sound distantly related to dǎo, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 她从小就学习舞蹈。
example.pinyin: Tā cóngxiǎo jiù xuéxí wǔdǎo.
example.english: She has studied dance since childhood.
example.fact: 舞蹈 doubles two characters that each independently mean "to dance": 舞 (pictured with a dancer's sleeves above and a pair of feet 舛 below) and 蹈 (足 "foot" plus a phonetic) — the same synonym-doubling strategy behind 拒绝 and 邀请 elsewhere in this batch.

components.note: 木 (tree) — relates directly to 根's meaning 'root (of a plant or tree).'
艮 (gèn) gives a sound hint — 根 is pronounced gēn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
扌 (hand) — relates to 据's meaning 'to rely on, according to,' as if grasping evidence in hand.
居 (jū) gave the base sound; the pronunciation later shifted to jù, keeping the same final but a different tone.

example.hanzi: 根据报告,今年的销售额有所增长。
example.pinyin: Gēnjù bàogào, jīnnián de xiāoshòu'é yǒusuǒ zēngzhǎng.
example.english: According to the report, this year's sales have increased somewhat.
example.fact: 根据 does double grammatical duty: a preposition ("according to," placed before a noun phrase, as here) and a countable noun ("a basis, grounds," as in 有根据 "well-founded," fittingly the classifier 个 is listed right in its own dictionary entry) — one more Chinese word that switches role for free where English often needs two different words.

components.note: 几 depicts a small low table or stool with legs — a simple domestic object.

example.hanzi: 他几乎每天都跑步。
example.pinyin: Tā jīhū měitiān dōu pǎobù.
example.english: He runs almost every day.
example.fact: 几 changes its reading depending on the word: jǐ means "how many, a few" (几个人, "how many/some people"), but in 几乎 and a small set of other words (茶几, "a small table") it is read jī instead — another case, like 恶心, where a character's reading has to be learned per word rather than derived from one rule.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — the material of ancient counting rods.
具 (held in two hands) — bamboo counting rods or an abacus held up for use, the tools of calculation that gave 算 its meaning 'to calculate, count.'
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.hanzi: 这道菜算是我们店里的招牌菜。
example.pinyin: Zhè dào cài suànshì wǒmen diàn lǐ de zhāopáicài.
example.english: This dish counts as our restaurant's signature dish.
example.fact: 算 already covers both "to calculate" and, more loosely, "to count as, to qualify as" — 算是 simply locks in that second, looser sense with 是 ("to be"), turning an arithmetic verb into a hedge for tentative or approximate classification ("counts as," "is more or less").

components.note: 木 (wood) — 案 originally referred to a wooden table or desk
安 (ān) gives a sound close to 案's reading àn, differing only in tone

example.hanzi: 这个问题的答案很简单。
example.pinyin: Zhège wèntí de dá'àn hěn jiǎndān.
example.english: The answer to this question is very simple.
example.fact: 答案 pairs the verb root 答 ("to answer, reply") with 案 ("a case, file, record"), giving the image of an answer as something formally set down — not unlike how English "case" and "file" both extend from physical documents to abstract records.

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'
⺈ (a person, bent over) — the figure whose outward expression is being depicted.
巴 — traditionally linked to desire or emotion, so together the character points to a person's expression or complexion, extended to 色's meaning 'color, appearance.'

example.hanzi: 他在这次比赛中表现得非常出色。
example.pinyin: Tā zài zhè cì bǐsài zhōng biǎoxiàn de fēicháng chūsè.
example.english: He performed extremely well in this competition.
example.fact: 出色 literally means "to step outside of [ordinary] color/hue" (出 "to emerge, exceed" plus 色 "color, appearance") — much like English "outstanding" (literally "standing out"), two unrelated languages independently reached for a spatial image of exceeding the ordinary to describe excellence.

components.note: 目 depicts an eye turned on its side, with the outline and pupil visible — later straightened into today's rectangular shape.

example.hanzi: 目前情况还不太清楚。
example.pinyin: Mùqián qíngkuàng hái bú tài qīngchǔ.
example.english: The situation is still not very clear at present.
example.fact: 目前 literally means "before the eye(s)" (目 "eye" + 前 "in front of") — the same spatial metaphor for the present moment recurs in 眼前 ("right before one's eyes," also meaning "right now"), built from a different "eye" character on the same logic.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 活 relates to water flowing, a symbol of life and vitality.
舌 (shé) gives a hint of the sound — 活 is pronounced huó, a connection that has shifted over time.
力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.

example.hanzi: 医生让我每天多活动活动。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng ràng wǒ měitiān duō huódòng huódòng.
example.english: The doctor told me to move around more every day.
example.fact: Reduplicating 活动 into 活动活动 softens it into a casual, low-commitment suggestion — "just move around a bit" — the same reduplication pattern seen in 谢谢 and 试试, where repeating a verb makes the action sound lighter and less demanding.

components.note: 林 here depicts eyes shut in sleep, not its usual meaning 'forest.'
夕 (evening, night) — sleeping at night is when dreams occur, giving 梦 its meaning 'dream.'
心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 成为一名医生是她的梦想。
example.pinyin: Chéngwéi yì míng yīshēng shì tā de mèngxiǎng.
example.english: Becoming a doctor is her dream.
example.fact: 梦想 (an aspiration, "dream" in the sense of a life goal) is a different word from 梦 alone or 做梦 (the literal dream one has while asleep) — English collapses both senses into a single word "dream," but Chinese keeps the sleep-dream and the aspiration mostly apart in everyday use.

components.note: 日 (sun) — 最 pictures something happening under the sun, that is, everywhere.
取 (to take, gather) — combined with the sun above, gathering everything under the sun gave 最 its meaning of 'most' or 'the utmost.'
纟 (thread) — 终 originally referred to the end of a woven thread, extended to mean 'end, final'
冬 (dōng) gives a loose sound connection to 终's reading zhōng

example.hanzi: 经过多次尝试,他最终成功了。
example.pinyin: Jīngguò duō cì chángshì, tā zuìzhōng chénggōng le.
example.english: After many attempts, he finally succeeded.
example.fact: 最 (built from 日 "sun" plus 取 "to take, gather" — everything gathered under the sun, i.e. "the utmost") is Chinese's core superlative marker, forming the "-est" of almost any adjective (最好 "best," 最大 "biggest") — 最终 simply applies that same superlative logic to 终 ("the end"), giving "the very last, final."

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 这个游乐场只适合大人,不适合小孩。
example.pinyin: Zhège yóulèchǎng zhǐ shìhé dàren, bú shìhé xiǎohái.
example.english: This amusement park is only suitable for adults, not children.
example.fact: As "adult, grownup" this word is read with a neutral tone, dàren; but in period dramas and formal historical address (roughly "your honor"), the same two characters are instead read dàrén, with a full second tone on 人 — a reading split not unlike how 东西 (also flagged in the pilot batch) shifts meaning between its toned and neutral-toned forms.

components.note: 再 depicts something stacked again on top of a base line — repetition, or doing something 'once more,' is pictured by piling on an extra layer.
冫 (originally a mark for repetition, unrelated to its later meaning 'ice') — suggests something done more than once.
欠 (a person yawning, mouth open) — repeated yawning gave 次 its meaning of a 'time' or occurrence, as in counting how many times something happens.

example.hanzi: 请再次确认您的信息。
example.pinyin: Qǐng zàicì quèrèn nín de xìnxī.
example.english: Please confirm your information once more.
example.fact: 再次 is a more formal, written-register synonym for the everyday adverb 再 ("again") — 请再次确认 ("please confirm again") reads like an instruction manual or official notice, whereas casual speech would simply say 再确认一下.

components.note: 旡 — a person turning their head away
皀 — a dish of food, already finished with
灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 既然你已经决定了,我就不再劝你了。
example.pinyin: Jìrán nǐ yǐjīng juédìng le, wǒ jiù bú zài quàn nǐ le.
example.english: Since you've already decided, I won't try to persuade you anymore.
example.fact: 既然 almost always sets up a matching 就 later in the sentence ("既然...,就...") to draw a conclusion from an accepted premise — a paired-clause structure much like "因为...,所以..." (also flagged in the pilot batch), where the first half states a given fact and the second draws what naturally follows.

components.note: A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.
贝 (shell/money — cowrie shells were historically used as currency) — 员 originally related to counting or officials responsible for accounts, later broadening to mean 'member' or 'personnel.'

example.hanzi: 请所有工作人员到会议室集合。
example.pinyin: Qǐng suǒyǒu gōngzuò rényuán dào huìyìshì jíhé.
example.english: Please have all staff members gather in the meeting room.
example.fact: 人员 rarely stands completely alone — it usually attaches to a role or department to specify which staff is meant, as in 工作人员 ("work personnel, staff") here or 医护人员 ("medical personnel"); bare 人员 by itself reads as oddly abstract, almost bureaucratic, in casual speech.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 英 originally meant 'flower, blossom,' later borrowed for 'outstanding, hero' and to write 'England, English.'
央 (yāng) gives a sound hint — 英 is pronounced yīng, sharing the initial consonant and a nasal final, though the vowel has shifted.
隹 (short-tailed bird) — 雄 originally described the male of a bird species, extending to 'male' generally and 'heroic, grand.'
厷 (gōng) gives a sound distantly related to xióng, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 他是很多孩子心中的英雄。
example.pinyin: Tā shì hěn duō háizi xīnzhōng de yīngxióng.
example.english: He is a hero in the hearts of many children.
example.fact: 雄's own component note explains that it originally described the male of a bird species (隹, "short-tailed bird") before extending to "male" generally and then to "heroic, grand" — a faint gendered echo still sitting underneath the modern, gender-neutral word for "hero."

components.note: 从 (two people, one following another) — depicts people together.
土 (earth/ground) — two people seated on the ground gave 坐 its meaning 'to sit.'
A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 请大家坐下。
example.pinyin: Qǐng dàjiā zuòxia.
example.english: Everyone, please sit down.
example.fact: 下 attached after a verb like 坐 acts as a directional complement marking downward motion completed (坐下 "sit down," 躺下 "lie down," 蹲下 "squat down") — a small, reusable verb-plus-direction pattern that turns a bare verb into a specific physical action with a clear endpoint.

components.note: 咸 (all, together) — 感 relates to a shared reaction.
心 (heart) — feelings that stir the heart gave 感 its meaning 'to feel' or 'emotion.'
爫 (a hand, from above) — 受 pictures something being passed.
又 (a hand, from below) — one hand giving and another receiving gave 受 its meaning 'to receive' or 'to endure.'

example.hanzi: 请说说你对这本书的感受。
example.pinyin: Qǐng shuōshuo nǐ duì zhè běn shū de gǎnshòu.
example.english: Please talk about your feelings about this book.
example.fact: 感受 names an inner, subjective impression formed through experience, while its near-synonym 感觉 leans more toward an immediate physical or intuitive sense ("it feels cold") — the two overlap heavily in casual speech, but 感受 skews slightly more reflective.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 件 relates to a person separating something into parts.
牛 (ox) — dividing an ox into pieces gave 件 its meaning of an individual 'item' or 'piece,' now used as a measure word for objects and matters.

example.hanzi: 这次事件引起了很多人的关注。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì shìjiàn yǐnqǐle hěn duō rén de guānzhù.
example.english: This incident drew a lot of people's attention.
example.fact: 事件 leans toward a notable, often newsworthy occurrence — a scandal, accident, or historic happening — while the more general noun 事情 ("affair, matter") covers any ordinary task; calling a minor errand a 事件 would sound oddly dramatic.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, movement) — 通 relates to passing through or getting somewhere.
甬 (yǒng) gives a hint of the sound — 通 is pronounced tōng, a connection that has shifted over time.
口 (mouth) — 知 relates to speaking what one knows.
矢 (shǐ) gives a hint of the sound — 知 is pronounced zhī, a connection that has faded over time.

example.hanzi: 学校已经通知了所有家长。
example.pinyin: Xuéxiào yǐjīng tōngzhīle suǒyǒu jiāzhǎng.
example.english: The school has already notified all the parents.
example.fact: 通知 works as both a verb ("to notify") and a noun ("a notice, notification") without changing form — like 工作 in the pilot batch, it's one more common case of a Chinese word doing double grammatical duty for free where English often needs two different words.

meanings: have no choice or option but to

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'
The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'

example.hanzi: 因为下雨,我们不得不取消野餐。
example.pinyin: Yīnwèi xiàyǔ, wǒmen bùdébù qǔxiāo yěcān.
example.english: Because it rained, we had no choice but to cancel the picnic.
example.fact: 不得不 is built from a double-negative logic — 不 (not) + 得 (able to) + 不 (not) — literally "not able to not [do it]," the same double-negative-makes-a-forced-positive structure behind English "can't help but" or "cannot not."

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 论 relates to discussing or explaining something with words.
仑 (logical order, arrangement) — combined with speech, 论 came to mean 'to discuss' or 'a theory,' explaining ideas in an orderly way.

example.hanzi: 无论发生什么,我都会支持你。
example.pinyin: Wúlùn fāshēng shénme, wǒ dōu huì zhīchí nǐ.
example.english: No matter what happens, I will support you.
example.fact: 无论 sets up a clause that almost always closes with 都 later on ("无论...,都...") to mean "regardless of X, the outcome is always Y" — like 所有...都... in the pilot batch, it's the trailing 都 that actually carries the "no exceptions" meaning, while 无论 just introduces the range of possibilities.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with an implement, action) — relates to 放's meaning 'to let go, release, put.'
方 (fāng) gives the sound — 放 is pronounced fàng, a close match sharing the same rhyme.
廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'

example.hanzi: 妈妈慢慢放开了孩子的手。
example.pinyin: Māma mànmàn fàngkāile háizi de shǒu.
example.english: The mother slowly let go of the child's hand.
example.fact: 放开 pairs the verb 放 ("to release, put down") with the resultative complement 开 ("apart, open") to spell out the outcome of releasing — grip loosens until the two things are apart — the same verb-plus-开 pattern shows up in 打开 ("to open") and 拉开 ("to pull apart"), a productive way Chinese verbs specify their result.

components.note: Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.hanzi: 后来,他搬到了北京。
example.pinyin: Hòulái, tā bāndàole Běijīng.
example.english: Afterwards, he moved to Beijing.
example.fact: 后来 can only point to a moment after some past reference point already established in the story or conversation — it cannot be used for the future the way English "later" sometimes can ("see you later" is never 后来见), which instead needs 以后 or 再见.

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — 适 relates to fitting well as one moves along, i.e. being suitable
舌 (shé) gives a sound distantly related to 适's reading shì, having drifted apart over a long time

example.hanzi: 这份工作很适合你。
example.pinyin: Zhè fèn gōngzuò hěn shìhé nǐ.
example.english: This job suits you very well.
example.fact: 适合 takes its object directly, with no preposition needed (这份工作适合你, literally "this job suits you") — English speakers learning Chinese sometimes mistakenly insert 对 or 给 before the object by analogy with "suit to/for someone," but 适合 already functions as a complete transitive verb on its own.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 许 relates to giving permission through words.
午 (wǔ) gives a hint of the sound — 许 is pronounced xǔ, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 这里不允许吸烟。
example.pinyin: Zhèlǐ bù yǔnxǔ xīyān.
example.english: Smoking is not allowed here.
example.fact: 允许 is the more formal, written-register cousin of the everyday verb 让 ("to let, allow") — official rules, signs, and contracts reach for 允许 (不允许吸烟, "smoking not permitted"), while spoken Chinese much more often just says 不让 or 不能.

components.note: 丿 (something falling) — an object slipping away.
夫 (a hand/person) — the object slipping out of a hand, giving 失 its meaning 'to lose.'
Depicts a person standing tall, gazing up at the moon 月 — the image of looking into the distance, the source of 望's meaning 'to gaze, hope, expect.'

example.hanzi: 听到这个消息,我很失望。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège xiāoxi, wǒ hěn shīwàng.
example.english: Hearing this news, I was very disappointed.
example.fact: 失望 literally means "to lose hope" (失 "to lose" + 望 "to gaze, hope, expect") — 望 is traditionally pictured as a person standing on tiptoe, gazing up at the moon, an image of looking hopefully into the distance that 失望 turns into its opposite: hope lost.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'

example.hanzi: 大家对这个计划有什么意见?
example.pinyin: Dàjiā duì zhège jìhuà yǒu shénme yìjiàn?
example.english: Does everyone have any opinions about this plan?
example.fact: 意见 covers both a neutral "opinion, viewpoint" and, in the fixed phrase 有意见 ("to have an objection, a complaint"), a sharper sense of disagreement or grievance — context alone decides which register is meant, since the same two characters serve both a mild and a critical reading.

components.note: 寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'

example.hanzi: 她在比赛中获得了第一名。
example.pinyin: Tā zài bǐsài zhōng huòdéle dì yī míng.
example.english: She won first place in the competition.
example.fact: 获得 sits at the more formal, written end of the "get, obtain" spectrum — used for winning awards or gaining abstract things like 支持 ("support") or 信任 ("trust") — while the everyday verb 得到 covers much the same ground in ordinary conversation.

components.note: 女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'
Traditionally analyzed as 日 combined with 疋, linked to the idea of speaking directly and truthfully — the source of 是's meaning 'to be, indeed, right.'

example.hanzi: 要是明天不下雨,我们就去爬山。
example.pinyin: Yàoshi míngtiān bú xiàyǔ, wǒmen jiù qù páshān.
example.english: If it doesn't rain tomorrow, we'll go hiking.
example.fact: 要是 is the casual, spoken-register twin of 如果 (also in the pilot batch) — both introduce a conditional clause and both commonly pair with a following 就, but 要是 sounds distinctly more colloquial and shows up far more in relaxed conversation than in formal writing.

components.note: 八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
宀 (roof) — 寓 names a place someone lives, a residence.
禺 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 寓, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 他们住在一间小公寓里。
example.pinyin: Tāmen zhù zài yì jiān xiǎo gōngyù lǐ.
example.english: They live in a small apartment.
example.fact: 公寓 literally pairs 公 ("public, shared") with 寓 ("a residence, a dwelling") — together painting a home that is not a private, standalone house but one unit within a larger, shared building, the core idea behind "apartment" in any language.

components.note: 文 depicts a chest marked with crossing lines, once tattoos or patterns on the body — decoration and pattern gave rise to the idea of 'writing' and 'culture.'
亻 (person) — 件 relates to a person separating something into parts.
牛 (ox) — dividing an ox into pieces gave 件 its meaning of an individual 'item' or 'piece,' now used as a measure word for objects and matters.

example.hanzi: 请把这份文件发给我。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ zhè fèn wénjiàn fā gěi wǒ.
example.english: Please send this document to me.
example.fact: 文件 extended naturally from paper documents into computing, where it is now also the standard word for a digital "file" — the same semantic shift English "file" itself went through, from a physical folder of papers to a unit of digital data.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the source of speech.
八 here suggests something small or simple leaving the mouth, giving 只 its meaning 'only, merely.'
Originally a drawing of a bear, with 厶 as its head, ⺼ as its body, and 匕匕 as its claws; the picture was later borrowed to mean 'ability, to be able to.'

example.hanzi: 因为票卖完了,我们只能站着看。
example.pinyin: Yīnwèi piào màiwán le, wǒmen zhǐnéng zhànzhe kàn.
example.english: Since the tickets sold out, we could only watch standing up.
example.fact: 只能 marks a constrained, no-better-option ability — "can only, forced to" — distinct from 能 alone, which stays neutral about whether other options exist; adding 只 turns a plain statement of capability into an implicit complaint about limited choices.

components.note: 彐 (a hand reaching out) — 寻 relates to searching, reaching for something.
寸 (cùn) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading xún has diverged.
扌 (hand) — represents an action performed by hand.
戈 (a spear/dagger-axe) — an old image of searching or probing with a weapon in hand, giving 找 its meaning 'to search, to look for.'

example.hanzi: 他一直在寻找失踪的猫。
example.pinyin: Tā yìzhí zài xúnzhǎo shīzōng de māo.
example.english: He has been searching for his missing cat all along.
example.fact: 寻找 is a more formal, written-feeling synonym for the everyday verb 找 alone ("to look for") — it doubles up two verbs that each independently mean "to search" (寻 and 找), the same reinforcing word-building strategy seen in 喜欢 and 舞蹈, elevating the register slightly above bare 找.

components.note: 攵 (an action/to strike) — 攻 relates directly to attacking or striking
工 (gōng) gives the sound — 攻 is also pronounced gōng, an exact match
手 (hand) — in the traditional form 擊, 手 contributed the meaning of striking with force, the source of 击's meaning 'to hit, strike.'

example.hanzi: 敌军突然发起了攻击。
example.pinyin: Dí jūn tūrán fāqǐle gōngjī.
example.english: The enemy army suddenly launched an attack.
example.fact: 攻击 covers both literal, physical attacks (military or otherwise) and abstract verbal ones (人身攻击, "a personal attack, an ad hominem") — much like English "attack" itself stretches from a punch to a cutting remark, Chinese did not need a separate word for the metaphorical extension either.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 快点出发,不然我们要迟到了。
example.pinyin: Kuài diǎn chūfā, bùrán wǒmen yào chídào le.
example.english: Let's leave quickly, or else we'll be late.
example.fact: 不然 literally means "not so" (不 "not" + 然 "so, thus") and sets up an unwanted alternative if a preceding suggestion is not followed — the same 然 that appears in 然后 ("then") and 突然 ("suddenly"), a character whose core sense of "in this manner" recurs across several common connectors.

components.note: Walk/movement — inviting someone often involves going to meet them.
Gives the sound jiǎo, related to yāo but drifted apart over time.
讠 (speech) — relates to 请's meaning 'to request, invite; please,' a spoken request.
青 (qīng) gives a sound hint — 请 is pronounced qǐng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 我们邀请了很多朋友来参加聚会。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yāoqǐngle hěn duō péngyou lái cānjiā jùhuì.
example.english: We invited a lot of friends to come to the party.
example.fact: 邀请 doubles two verbs that already independently mean roughly "to invite, request" — 邀 ("to invite, entreat") and 请 ("please, to request") — the same reinforcing two-near-synonym pattern behind 舞蹈 and 寻找 elsewhere in this set.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 管 originally referred to a bamboo pipe or tube, later broadening to mean 'to manage' or 'to control.'
官 (guān) gives a hint of the sound — 管 is pronounced guǎn, a connection that has shifted only slightly in tone.

example.hanzi: 尽管天气很冷,他还是坚持出去跑步。
example.pinyin: Jǐnguǎn tiānqì hěn lěng, tā háishi jiānchí chūqù pǎobù.
example.english: Although the weather was very cold, he still insisted on going out for a run.
example.fact: 尽管 sets up a concessive clause that typically pairs with 还是 or 但是 later on ("尽管...,还是...") to mean "even though X, Y still happens" — the same paired-clause logic recurs throughout this batch's connectors, including the 既然...就... and 无论...都... constructions.
